metadata.title: What are the Factors Affecting Turkish Students’ Science Literacy? A Hierarchical Linear Modelling Study Using PISA 2015 Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 Turkey microdata with a stratified random sampling design at the student level (12 regions, 61 cities, 187 schools; 5895 students). The analysis is conducted with HLM 7 to account for the nested structure of students within schools, motivated by a high intraclass correlation (ICC = 0.52). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure, so it is unclear whether complex-survey weighting was applied in estimation. The analytic sample appears to be the full available Turkey sample for the specified age group (15-year-olds), with variable selection based on bivariate correlations (excluding highly collinear variables with r > 0.7) and retaining only statistically significant predictors in the final level-1 and level-2 models.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that each student has 10 science plausible values and that the analysis uses an approach based on averaging plausible values to obtain a single score per student, but it does not describe any missing-data strategy for questionnaire/index variables or for the plausible values themselves. Because the dependent variable is PV-based science literacy, missingness handling is methodologically important; the absence of a documented procedure represents a reporting gap rather than a design feature. Without knowing whether cases were excluded or imputed, the robustness of the reported coefficients and variance explained cannot be fully assessed.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2015 Turkey sample of 15-year-old students (5895 students) drawn via stratified random sampling across 12 regions, 61 cities, and 187 schools. The dependent variable is science literacy based on plausible values; the paper indicates that averaging across plausible values is used to create a single score per student. For model building, indices were screened using bivariate correlations and only one variable was retained among pairs with high collinearity (r > 0.7); for example, among ESCS components, only ESCS was included while HEDRES was excluded. Finally, only statistically significant predictors were retained in the level-1 (student) and level-2 (school) models.

main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM null model mean (intercept): 425.15 (SE=4.96, t=85.77, p<0.001). Within-school variance reduced from 2872.79 (null) to 2505.95 (level-1), explaining 12.77% of within-school variance. Level-1 significant coefficients: Gender 10.94 (p<0.001), Class level 14.89 (p<0.001), Grade repetition -18.95 (p=0.001), ESCS 2.33 (p=0.024), Out-of-school study time -0.34 (p<0.001), Weekly science learning time 0.09 (p<0.001), Weekly total instruction time 0.01 (p=0.028), Enjoyment of cooperation 5.34 (p<0.001), Inquiry-based science teaching -3.79 (p<0.001). Between-school variance reduced from 3056.81 (null) to 2056.10 (level-2), explaining 32.74% of between-school variance. Level-2 significant coefficients: Internet-connected computer ratio 40.95 (p=0.016), Science teachers ratio 214.15 (p=0.016), Science-specific resources total 6.89 (p<0.001), Learning-hindering student behavior -13.19 (p=0.003).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science literacy data for Turkish 15-year-olds, the study leveraged weekly science learning time, science-specific resources, out-of-school study time, ESCS, and inquiry-based science teaching to model science literacy, finding that weekly science learning time and science-specific resources were the strongest positive predictors while out-of-school study time and inquiry-based science teaching showed significant negative associations. This indicates that policy should prioritize in-school, science-focused instructional time and science resource provision (especially in disadvantaged schools) rather than expanding out-of-school study time or assuming inquiry-based teaching automatically improves science literacy, while also recognizing that the study is associational and uses averaged PV scores.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 science literacy for Turkey (15-year-olds; N=5895 students from 187 schools) using hierarchical linear modeling (HLM 7) to address the nested student-within-school structure (ICC=0.52). The authors report that averaging across the 10 science plausible values yields a single PV-based science literacy score per student. In the level-1 (student) model, nine student-level variables explain 12.77% of within-school variance; the strongest student predictor is weekly science learning time, while out-of-school study time is significantly negative and inquiry-based science teaching is also negative. In the level-2 (school) model, four school-level variables explain 32.74% of between-school variance; science-specific resources are the strongest positive school predictor. The paper does not report a missing-data strategy or whether PISA sampling/replicate weights were applied, limiting interpretability of effect sizes and generalizability.
